A_identity.qualification_type: Secondary school-leaving diploma (diplôme national) that is simultaneously the standard gateway credential to French higher education; treated as a single unified qualification_type = 'national_secondary_leaving_exam_and_university_entry_credential'.
A_identity.source_notes: education.gouv.fr and eduscol.education.gouv.fr blocked direct automated fetch (HTTP 403) during this research; facts below are corroborated across multiple independent secondary sources (L'Étudiant, digiSchool, Cours Legendre, Capitaine Study) that explicitly cite and quote the Ministry's own published coefficient tables, plus the Ministry's own page title 'Comment calculer votre note au baccalauréat' confirmed to exist via search indexing. Confidence: high, but flagged as secondary-source-corroborated rather than directly fetched.

B_grading_model.scale: 0 to 20, in accordance with the standard French academic grading convention used throughout French primary, secondary, and higher education (not Bac-specific, but the scale the Bac uses).
B_grading_model.passing_threshold: 10/20 overall average to obtain the diplôme.

mention_thresholds.tres_bien: 16.00–20/20 (mention 'Très Bien avec félicitations du jury' can be awarded at the jury's discretion for the highest results, typically ≥18)

B_grading_model.confidence: high — thresholds are stable/long-standing and consistently reported across every independent source checked, but exact wording of the 'félicitations du jury' discretionary sub-mention was not independently verified against a primary Ministry document in this session and should be treated as medium confidence on that specific detail only.
B_grading_model.explicit_rule_reminder: Do NOT invent a GPA/4.0 conversion for the 0-20 scale. No authoritative French or US source found in this research states an official cross-scale conversion for the Bac; unofficial conversion tables exist only on GPA-converter marketing sites (e.g., SmartCGPA) which are not authoritative and should not be treated as ground truth by ORYN.

C_structure_concepts.current_structure_effective_since: First examined in session 2021 (reform announced 2018, phased in starting with students entering première in September 2019). This is the CURRENT structure — the old filière S/ES/L system was abolished and must not be described as current.
C_structure_concepts.tronc_commun_common_core: Français (assessed via 'épreuves anticipées de français' — written + oral — at the end of première), Histoire-Géographie, Langue Vivante A & B, Enseignement scientifique, Éducation physique et sportive (EPS), Enseignement moral et civique, and Philosophie (terminale only, examined via a national written exam in June).
C_structure_concepts.specialites: Students choose 3 'enseignements de spécialité' (specialty subjects, 4h/week each) at the start of première from a Ministry-defined list (Mathématiques, Physique-Chimie, SVT, SES, Histoire-Géographie/géopolitique/sciences politiques (HGGSP), Humanités/Littérature/Philosophie, Langues/Littératures/Cultures étrangères, Numérique et sciences informatiques, Arts, and others depending on lycée offerings). At the end of première, one spécialité is dropped; the remaining 2 are continued through terminale (6h/week each) and examined via written national exams held in March of terminale.
C_structure_concepts.grand_oral: A oral examination in terminale (introduced by the 2021 reform) where the student presents and defends a project connected to one or both of their retained spécialités, before a jury.
C_structure_concepts.controle_continu_vs_epreuves_terminales: Overall Bac grade = 40% contrôle continu (average of grades recorded in the student's bulletins/livret scolaire across première and terminale — NOT standardized common tests; the earlier 'E3C' standardized-common-test model used in 2019–2021 was abandoned in favor of straightforward bulletin averages starting session 2022) + 60% épreuves terminales (final national exams: French written+oral, philosophy, the two spécialité exams, and the grand oral).

coefficients_confirmed.grand_oral: 10 for sessions through 2026; the coefficient is set to change to 8 starting session 2027, when a new anticipated mathematics exam (coefficient 2) is introduced for students not taking a math-related spécialité — verify against the Ministry's session-specific coefficient table before relying on this for a 2027+ cohort.

C_structure_concepts.confidence: high on the overall 40/60 split and specialty/tronc-commun structure (consistently corroborated); medium on the precise 2027 coefficient change, which was reported by secondary sources referencing a planned reform and should be re-verified closer to that session.

D_rigor_signals.primary_signal: Choice of spécialités relative to the student's intended field of study is the main academic-rigor/fit signal in the French system — e.g., a student targeting engineering typically retains Mathématiques + Physique-Chimie; a student targeting economics/social science typically retains SES + Mathématiques or HGGSP.
D_rigor_signals.secondary_signal: Performance on the spécialité national written exams (taken in terminale, weighted heavily in épreuves terminales) is a stronger external rigor signal than contrôle continu bulletin averages alone, since it is externally graded rather than teacher-graded.
D_rigor_signals.no_oryn_score_invented: This research does not propose or imply any ORYN-internal numeric rigor score; it only identifies which native signals (spécialité choice, spécialité exam results) are meaningful for a counselor to read.

E_predicted_grades.formal_predicted_grade_concept: No formal, UK-style 'predicted grade' concept exists in the French Bac system for domestic use. Verified: the French university admissions platform Parcoursup does not ask for or generate numeric predicted final grades. Instead it uses the 'livret scolaire' (record of actual première/terminale bulletin grades, including first-année Bac component grades already sat) plus a qualitative 'Fiche Avenir' containing the lycée's class council opinion on the student's likely success in higher education, expressed on a qualitative 4-point scale ('très favorable', 'favorable', 'assez favorable', 'réservé') — not a numeric grade prediction.
E_predicted_grades.caveat_for_non_french_admissions: When French Bac students apply to universities outside France (e.g., UK, US) before their final Bac results are known, their lycée may informally supply anticipated/estimated grades for that specific foreign application — but this is an ad hoc accommodation for the receiving country's process, not a formal component of the French Bac system itself. Do not treat this as equivalent to a UK A-Level predicted grade.
E_predicted_grades.confidence: high on the core finding (no formal domestic predicted-grade mechanism); the informal foreign-application caveat is a reasonable inference by analogy to the confirmed German Abitur pattern (see other system) rather than a directly sourced French-specific citation, so flagged medium confidence on that specific caveat.

F_class_rank.finding: Class rank ('rang') is not a formal, Ministry-mandated element of the French Bac diploma or of the national transcript, but per-subject rank-in-class is commonly auto-generated and displayed on bulletins by school software (e.g., Pronote) as an informal pedagogical/internal statistic, and some lycées choose to surface it, partly discussed in connection with what appears on Parcoursup dossiers. It is inconsistent and school-dependent, not a uniform national practice with a fixed definition.
F_class_rank.source_quality: medium — based on teacher-forum and software-documentation discussion (Neoprofs, Index-Éducation/Pronote documentation) rather than a Ministry policy statement; no authoritative Ministry source found either confirming or banning class rank reporting.
F_class_rank.oryn_rule_reminder: Never infer or fabricate a French student's class rank from grades alone. If 'rang' is not present in the student's notes/transcript text, treat it as unknown, not absent-therefore-irrelevant and not computable from GPA.

G_external_assessment.finding: The Bac exams themselves (spécialité written exams in March of terminale, French written+oral at end of première, philosophy and grand oral in June of terminale) ARE the primary external/standardized assessment in the French system — there is no separate national school-leaving test distinct from the Bac, and no separate SAT/ACT-equivalent is part of the French secondary system. Some French students additionally sit external tests (e.g., TOEFL/IELTS, or the SAT for students also applying to the US) but these are optional and unrelated to the Bac itself.

H_unsafe_inferences: Do not cross-convert a 0-20 Bac average or bulletin grade into a US-style 4.0 GPA — no authoritative French or US source supports an official conversion; only unofficial marketing-site tables exist.

Do not assume a French Bac 'mention' (Assez Bien / Bien / Très Bien) maps to any specific US GPA band — mentions are computed on an entirely different scale and grading culture (French grading is famously stringent; a 14/20 'Bien' reflects strong performance despite being 70% numerically).

Do not assume a missing class rank means the school does not track it, and equally do not assume its absence means nothing — French rank practice is inconsistent and school-software-dependent; treat as genuinely unknown unless present in source data.
Do not treat the Fiche Avenir's qualitative class-council opinion ('favorable', etc.) as a numeric predicted grade — it is categorically different information.
Do not describe the pre-2019 filière S/ES/L system as the current structure — it was replaced by the spécialités system starting with the 2021 exam session.

Do not assume every French secondary student outside metropolitan France (e.g., AEFE lycées abroad, including in Turkey) follows an identical local implementation — verify which specific Bac track (Général/Technologique) and spécialités a given school offers before assuming.

should_care_about: Which 2 spécialités the student retained through terminale, and how well those align with their stated target field/major (e.g., Mathématiques+Physique-Chimie for engineering targets vs. SES+HGGSP for social-science/policy targets).
Spécialité exam results specifically (externally graded, higher-signal than contrôle continu bulletin averages).
The mention achieved (Passable/Assez Bien/Bien/Très Bien) as a broad native-scale summary signal, reported as-is, never converted.
The qualitative Fiche Avenir / class council language if present in the student's record, as a native-context reference signal — not a number.
should_not_do: Fabricate a GPA-equivalent for the Bac average.
Assume or compute a class rank when not explicitly present.
Treat contrôle continu bulletin averages as equivalent in rigor/signal-strength to the externally graded spécialité exams.
Assume UK-style predicted grades exist for French Parcoursup admissions.

J_profile_data_model_implications.fits_existing_schema_how: education_records.curriculum currently has no 'french_baccalaureate' enum value, so a French Bac record must fall into 'national_curriculum' (semantically closest — France genuinely has one unified national curriculum/exam, unlike the US) with the specific 'Baccalauréat Général, spécialités: X, Y' detail placed in notes (free text). overall_gpa/gpa_scale should either be left null (correctly reflecting that the Bac does not use a GPA) or, if the school also happens to report a bulletin-average-derived GPA-like figure, gpa_scale should be recorded as 20 (never coerced to 4.0) with overall_gpa as the native 0-20 average, consistent with ORYN's existing no-cross-conversion rule. courses.grade_scale (TEXT) is well-suited to hold '/20' natively per course; courses.level enum has no 'spécialité' value, so spécialité courses currently have to be recorded as 'regular' or 'other', which loses the fact that a spécialité is the single highest-rigor course category in the French system (roughly analogous in significance to an AP/IB HL course, but the enum doesn't capture that equivalence).
gaps: No explicit 'french_baccalaureate' value in the curriculum enum — currently indistinguishable from any other country's generic 'national_curriculum' entry (e.g., could be confused with a Turkish national curriculum record) without reading free-text notes.

No 'specialite' (or generic 'advanced/highest-track') value in the courses.level enum, so a student's 2 retained spécialités cannot be structurally distinguished from a regular tronc-commun course without notes.

No field to record the 'mention' (Assez Bien/Bien/Très Bien) as a distinct structured native-scale achievement separate from overall_gpa — it currently would have to live in notes or be approximated numerically, risking conflation with a GPA-like number.

systems.system_name: German Abitur / DSD (Deutsches Sprachdiplom) — two distinct credentials

A_identity.system_name_abitur: Abitur (Allgemeine Hochschulreife) — the German general higher-education entrance qualification, earned via the gymnasiale Oberstufe (upper secondary level) and the Abiturprüfung (Abitur examination).
A_identity.system_name_dsd: Deutsches Sprachdiplom der Kultusministerkonferenz (DSD) — a German-as-a-foreign-language proficiency certificate. NOT the same credential as the Abitur (see dsd_vs_abitur_distinction below).
A_identity.owner_authority_abitur: Education in Germany is constitutionally a matter for the 16 individual Bundesländer (federal states); each state's Kultusministerium sets detailed rules, while the Kultusministerkonferenz (KMK) — the standing conference of the state ministers — issues nationwide framework agreements (e.g., the 'Vereinbarung zur Gestaltung der gymnasialen Oberstufe und der Abiturprüfung') to keep the Abitur broadly comparable across states. There is no single federal ministry that 'owns' the Abitur.
A_identity.owner_authority_dsd: The DSD is administered jointly by the Zentralstelle für das Auslandsschulwesen (ZfA — Central Agency for Schools Abroad, part of the German Federal Office of Administration/Bundesverwaltungsamt), under the authority of the Auswärtiges Amt (German Federal Foreign Office), in coordination with the KMK's Central DSD Committee. This is a DIFFERENT institutional pathway from the state-level Kultusministerien that issue the Abitur — the DSD is specifically a foreign-affairs/schools-abroad program, not a domestic state-school-leaving qualification.
A_identity.countries_contexts: Abitur: Germany (all 16 states) and German schools abroad that offer a full Abitur track (including some schools in Turkey, e.g., Deutsche Schule Istanbul, and German-partnership Anadolu lisesi programs). DSD: ~1,000+ partner schools ('DSD-Schulen') in roughly 65 countries worldwide, including numerous schools in Turkey (e.g., several Anadolu Lisesi campuses in Istanbul plus other schools with German as first foreign language) — confirmed via the Auswärtiges Amt's Turkey-specific page (tuerkei.diplo.de).

qualification_type.abitur: Secondary school-leaving diploma + general higher-education entrance qualification (Allgemeine Hochschulreife)
qualification_type.dsd_i: German-language proficiency certificate, CEFR range A2–B1 (candidate is certified at whichever level, A2 or B1, they actually reach)
qualification_type.dsd_ii: German-language proficiency certificate, CEFR range B2–C1

B_grading_model.regular_school_grades_1_to_6: Standard German school grading throughout secondary education uses a 1–6 scale where 1 = sehr gut (best) and 6 = ungenügend (fail); this is the grading convention used for ordinary coursework and report cards (Zeugnisse) generally, including below the Oberstufe.
B_grading_model.abitur_points_scale_0_to_15: In the gymnasiale Oberstufe (final two years, the Qualifikationsphase) and for the Abiturprüfung itself, a SEPARATE and DISTINCT 0–15 point scale ('Notenpunkte') is used, uniformly regulated nationwide by the KMK's upper-secondary-level agreement. Mapping: 15–13 points = grade 1 (sehr gut), 12–10 = grade 2 (gut), 9–7 = grade 3 (befriedigend), 6–4 = grade 4 (ausreichend), 3–1 = grade 5 (mangelhaft), 0 = grade 6 (ungenügend). Each of the six letter-grade bands is further subdivided into three point values (roughly corresponding to +/base/− tendencies), producing the 15-point granularity.
B_grading_model.final_abiturnote_calculation: The overall Abitur grade (Abiturnote, on the familiar 1.0–4.0/6.0 German scale students and universities recognize, where 1.0 is best) is computed from a weighted combination of (a) accumulated points from courses across the two-year Qualifikationsphase and (b) the results of the Abiturprüfung final exams. Per the KMK's own March 2023 press release on the upper-secondary agreement, qualification-phase coursework performance contributes two-thirds and the Abitur examination results contribute one-third of the overall qualification calculation (Gesamtqualifikation, Block I + Block II structure) — this is the figure corroborated by the KMK press release; a prior automated PDF-extraction attempt in this session produced a conflicting 40/60 split that could not be verified against readable source text and should be disregarded as unreliable, non-primary-sourced output.
B_grading_model.confidence: high on the existence of two distinct scales (1-6 for ordinary grades, 0-15 for Oberstufe/Abitur); medium-high on the exact two-thirds/one-third Gesamtqualifikation split (sourced from a KMK press release summary, not a directly-read primary legal text, due to PDF-fetch limitations in this session) — recommend a follow-up verification pass against the KMK's actual 'Vereinbarung' text if this precise ratio becomes product-critical.
B_grading_model.explicit_rule_reminder: No authoritative source found stating an official Abitur-to-US-GPA conversion. Do not invent one. The 1-6 and 0-15 scales must be preserved natively, never coerced into a 4.0 scale.

C_structure_concepts.leistungskurs_grundkurs: Students in the Qualifikationsphase take subjects at one of two levels: Leistungskurs (LK — advanced/elevated level, 'erhöhtes Anforderungsniveau', more instructional hours) and Grundkurs (GK — basic level, 'grundlegendes Anforderungsniveau'). This LK/GK terminology remains CURRENT as of 2026. Historically the number of LKs required varied by state (commonly 2, sometimes up to 3-4 depending on state); a KMK reform agreed in March 2023 standardizes this nationwide to 2 or 3 Leistungskurse (with double-weighting when there are only 2), but takes effect only for students entering the Qualifikationsphase in 2027 (first affected Abitur session: 2030) — so as of today (August 2026), the pre-reform, more state-variable LK/GK rules are still what is actually in effect for currently-enrolled students, and this transition should be tracked going forward.
C_structure_concepts.abiturpruefung: The final Abitur examination: written exams in a set of subjects (increasingly drawn, since 2023, 50% from a shared multi-state common exam item pool for German/Mathematics/first foreign language, extended to natural sciences from 2025, to improve cross-state comparability) plus typically an oral exam component (Kolloquium/mündliche Prüfung) in at least one subject.
C_structure_concepts.dsd_structure: The DSD is NOT a curriculum or course-credit system at all — it is a stand-alone examination (4 equally-weighted components: Reading Comprehension, Listening Comprehension, Written Communication, Oral Communication) that a student at a DSD-partner school sits, typically after a dedicated 'Deutsch als Fremdsprache' (DaF) preparatory course track, independent of whether that school also offers a German Abitur pathway.
C_structure_concepts.dsd_vs_abitur_distinction: These are categorically different credentials issued by categorically different authorities, and one does NOT imply the other. The DSD (issued via ZfA/Auswärtiges Amt/KMK's Central DSD Committee) certifies ONLY German-language proficiency (DSD I ≈ A2/B1 CEFR; DSD II ≈ B2/C1 CEFR) — per the KMK's own English-language page: 'Level A2/B1 of the [DSD I] is considered ... as proof that the pupil has reached a level of ability in German that is required for entry to a Studienkolleg,' and DSD II 'serves as proof of the German language proficiency required for studying at a university in Germany.' Neither statement says DSD confers the Abitur itself or any academic secondary-leaving qualification — it only proves language readiness, most commonly as a prerequisite to pursue German higher education, NOT as the academic qualification itself. A school can be DSD-authorized and have students earn DSD I/II WITHOUT any of them earning a German Abitur at all (the vast majority of DSD candidates globally — ~85,000/year across 65 countries — are at schools that do not offer a German Abitur track; DSD there functions like a language certificate such as TestDaF, alongside a wholly separate local/national diploma, e.g., a student could hold DSD II AND a standard Turkish Milli Eğitim diploma with no German Abitur involved at all). Separately, SOME schools (including, per this research, Deutsche Schule Istanbul) run students through BOTH the DSD II exam AND a full German Abitur or a recognized dual/international pathway toward one — e.g., the 'Deutsches Internationales Abitur' (DIA) offered at Deutsche Schule Istanbul, or the GIB ('Gemischtsprachiges Internationales Baccalaureat') model used at some Turkish Anadolu Lisesi campuses (e.g., ALKEV Özel Anadolu Lisesi, İELEV Okulları), which is a KMK/IB-co-developed bilingual IB Diploma variant taught partly in German (at least one language course plus subjects like History and Biology or Theory of Knowledge in German) that IS treated as equivalent in effect to an Abitur for German university access, per school-published descriptions — but this GIB/IB-hybrid pathway is itself DIFFERENT from BOTH a plain DSD and a plain domestic German Abitur, and should be recorded as its own distinct pathway, not conflated with either. A student's record showing 'DSD II' alone means language proficiency only; a record showing 'DSD II + Abitur' or 'DSD II + DIA' or 'GIB Diploma' means a materially different, stronger academic outcome and must not be treated as interchangeable with DSD alone.
C_structure_concepts.confidence: high on the core DSD≠Abitur distinction (directly sourced from KMK's own page); medium on the GIB/DIA specifics, which rely on school-published marketing/informational pages (ALKEV, İELEV, Deutsche Schule Istanbul) rather than a primary KMK/Turkish MEB regulatory document — recommend treating GIB/DIA program details as provisional pending a primary-source check, though the core fact that they are distinct from plain DSD is well corroborated.

D_rigor_signals.primary_signal: Which subjects a student chose as Leistungskurse (advanced level) relative to their intended field is the main native rigor/fit signal — analogous in function to spécialité choice in France or HL subject choice in IB.
D_rigor_signals.secondary_signal: Overall Abiturnote (final 1.0–4.0/6.0-scale grade) as a compressed native summary figure, always reported on its native scale.
D_rigor_signals.no_oryn_score_invented: No ORYN-internal numeric rigor score is proposed here — only the native signals to read (LK choice, Abiturnote, and — separately — any DSD level as an independent language-proficiency data point, never merged into an academic rigor score).

E_predicted_grades.domestic_finding: No formal predicted-grade concept exists for German university admission itself — German public universities generally will not admit on the basis of predicted results and expect the actual Abiturzeugnis (final Abitur certificate) after results are issued; some limited 'conditional admission' provisions exist mainly for applicants whose home-country diploma is academically shorter than the German 13-year track, which is a different mechanism from a UK-style predicted-grade offer.
E_predicted_grades.cross_border_finding: When German Abitur students apply to universities OUTSIDE Germany (UK/US, whose application deadlines fall before Abitur results are released), their school will informally provide an estimated/anticipated grade for that specific foreign application — this is an accommodation for the receiving country's process, not a formal feature of the German Abitur system itself, structurally parallel to the equivalent French finding.
E_predicted_grades.confidence: medium — sourced from general secondary discussion (McMillan Education International, conditional-admission explainer sites) rather than a primary KMK or German university-consortium document; treat as a reasonable, well-corroborated finding but not exhaustively primary-sourced.

F_class_rank.finding: Class rank is generally NOT a feature of German school culture or reporting — no authoritative source found stating German schools compute or publish a 'Klassenrangliste' as a standard transcript element, and general German-grading-culture sources describe grading as individually norm-referenced against fixed standards rather than peer-ranked. This is a genuine, expected cross-cultural difference from the US pattern and should be reported honestly as 'generally absent' rather than forced to fit a US-style expectation.
F_class_rank.confidence: medium — this is an absence-of-evidence finding (no source affirmatively describes German class ranking as a practice) rather than an explicit primary-source statement that it is prohibited or never done; treat as 'not a standard/expected feature,' not as an ironclad universal rule, since individual schools could theoretically vary.
F_class_rank.oryn_rule_reminder: Never infer or fabricate a German student's class rank. Its absence from a record should be read as normal/expected for this system, not as a data gap to fill.

G_external_assessment.finding: The Abiturprüfung (Abitur examination itself) IS the external/standardized assessment in the German system — written exams increasingly drawn from a shared multi-state item pool (50% for core subjects since 2023, extended to sciences from 2025) plus an oral component. The DSD exam is a SEPARATE external assessment (administered by ZfA-appointed examiners, not classroom teachers) measuring language proficiency only, and is not part of the Abiturprüfung even at schools offering both.

H_unsafe_inferences: Do NOT equate DSD (any level) with a German Abitur — DSD certifies German-language proficiency only, issued by a different authority (ZfA/Auswärtiges Amt/KMK Central DSD Committee) than the state Kultusministerien that issue the Abitur, and the large majority of DSD holders worldwide never earn a German Abitur at all.

Do not assume a student's school being 'DSD-authorized' or a 'Deutsche Schule' means that student's own diploma is a German Abitur — verify what specific credential(s) that individual student's record actually states (DSD only / DSD + Abitur / DSD + DIA / GIB Diploma / a plain Turkish Milli Eğitim diploma with a German-language elective, etc.) rather than inferring from the school's name or general reputation.
Do not cross-convert the 1-6 or 0-15 German scales into a US 4.0 GPA — no authoritative conversion source found.

Do not assume the pre-2023-reform LK/GK rules (which are what's actually in effect for currently enrolled students as of August 2026) are already replaced by the 2027-effective standardization — the new rules only bind cohorts entering the Qualifikationsphase in 2027 onward.
Do not infer or fabricate a German student's class rank; its typical absence from German records reflects the system's culture, not missing data.

Do not assume the GIB (Gemischtsprachiges Internationales Baccalaureat) offered at some Turkish schools is identical to either a plain IB Diploma or a plain German Abitur — treat it as its own distinct hybrid credential pending primary-source confirmation of its precise recognition status.

should_care_about: Which Leistungskurse the student chose, relative to their intended field of study.
The final Abiturnote on its native 1.0–4.0/6.0 scale.

A DSD level (I or II) as an independent, separately meaningful language-proficiency credential — genuinely useful signal for German-language readiness or Germany-bound study plans, but reported and reasoned about SEPARATELY from academic/curriculum strength, never merged into one score.
Whether a student's specific pathway is DSD-only, DSD+Abitur, DSD+DIA, or a GIB Diploma — these are materially different outcomes that change what the record actually proves.
should_not_do: Treat a DSD credential (at any level) as equivalent to fluency-plus-Abitur or as proof of a completed German secondary academic qualification.
Fabricate a GPA conversion for either German scale.
Assume or infer a class rank.
Assume a school's general German-partnership reputation tells you an individual student's actual credential — always read the specific record.

J_profile_data_model_implications.fits_existing_schema_how: education_records.curriculum has no 'german_abitur' value; a plain German Abitur record would currently have to go into 'national_curriculum' (reasonable fit — Germany does have a state-coordinated, KMK-harmonized national-level qualification, even though administration is state-level) or 'other', with 'Abitur, Leistungskurse: X, Y' captured only in free-text notes. overall_gpa/gpa_scale should be populated with the native Abiturnote and gpa_scale=either 6 (for the 1-6 letter-grade equivalent) or left null with the 0-15 Notenpunkte figure placed in notes/courses instead — ORYN should pick ONE native representation and document it consistently rather than mixing the two German scales into the same overall_gpa field, since 1-6 and 0-15 are not simply linearly interchangeable at the granular level (each 1-6 band spans 3 point-values). courses.level enum has no 'leistungskurs'/'grundkurs' distinction; LK courses currently have no clean home (closest existing value is 'honors', which is a US-culture-specific label that doesn't map cleanly onto the German system's own terminology and may mislead a counselor scanning course levels).
J_profile_data_model_implications.dsd_fit_assessment: DSD does NOT belong in education_records or as a 'curriculum' value at all — it is not a curriculum, it's a proficiency exam. Two reasonable homes exist in the current schema: (1) test_scores, with test_name='DSD I' or 'DSD II', score = the CEFR level actually attained (e.g., 'B1' or 'B2/C1'), and — this is a genuinely good fit — subscores (jsonb) can cleanly hold the DSD's own 4 equally-weighted components, e.g. {"reading":"B1","listening":"B1","writing":"A2","speaking":"B1"}, which maps naturally onto the DSD's actual structure; test_date = the exam sitting date. This is ORYN's honest recommendation: test_scores is a reasonable, not-forced fit for DSD, better than trying to wedge it into courses or education_records. (2) A secondary, weaker option would be a 'courses' row with subject='German language proficiency' and grade_value=the CEFR level, but this loses the exam's external/standardized nature (courses.grade_value implies a class grade, not an external certification) and is NOT recommended over test_scores.
gaps: No explicit 'german_abitur' curriculum enum value — currently indistinguishable from any other country's 'national_curriculum' entry without free-text notes.
No enum value distinguishing Leistungskurs from Grundkurs in courses.level — the closest existing value ('honors') is a mismatched cultural label.

No structured field to distinguish DSD-only vs. DSD+Abitur vs. DSD+DIA vs. GIB-Diploma pathways — since these are materially different outcomes, and a school registry lookup alone cannot disambiguate them, this is worth flagging as a real interpretive risk if ORYN's advisor logic ever tries to infer academic strength purely from 'has a DSD record' without checking whether a corresponding Abitur/DIA/GIB education_record also exists for the same student.

matrix_row.curriculum_qualification_exam: German Abitur (Allgemeine Hochschulreife) — DISTINCT from DSD (Deutsches Sprachdiplom, a language-proficiency-only certificate)
matrix_row.native_grading_scale: 1–6 (ordinary school grades, 1=best) for general coursework; separate 0–15 Notenpunkte scale for Oberstufe/Abiturprüfung, combining into a 1.0–4.0/6.0 Abiturnote; DSD uses its own CEFR-level scale (A2/B1 for DSD I, B2/C1 for DSD II), unrelated to the Abitur scales

unresolved_questions: Exact primary-source text of the KMK's 'two-thirds Qualifikationsphase / one-third Abiturprüfung' Gesamtqualifikation formula could not be directly read in this session (PDF fetch tooling limitation) — sourced instead from a KMK press-release summary; recommend a follow-up direct-document check if this exact ratio becomes load-bearing for any ORYN scoring logic.

Precise current (pre-2027-reform) number of required Leistungskurse in each of the 16 individual Bundesländer was not enumerated state-by-state in this session — only the general 'commonly 2, sometimes up to 3-4, state-variable' pattern and the 2027 standardization plan were confirmed.

The GIB (Gemischtsprachiges Internationales Baccalaureat) program's exact formal recognition status relative to the standard Abitur (i.e., whether it is legally treated as fully equivalent for all German university-admission purposes, or only for certain programs/states) was sourced only from school-published pages (ALKEV, İELEV), not a primary KMK or Turkish MEB regulatory document — recommend a dedicated follow-up if ORYN's Turkey school registry needs to certify GIB-Abitur-equivalence claims precisely.

systems.system_name: US High School Diploma / Transcript System

A_identity.system_name: US High School Diploma — there is explicitly NO single national diploma, curriculum, or grading system.
A_identity.owner_authority: No single national authority. Under the US federal system, K-12 education policy is constitutionally reserved primarily to the individual states (50 states + DC + territories), each with its own State Department/Board of Education setting minimum graduation requirements; within most states, further discretion is delegated down to local school districts and even individual schools for total credit counts, grading scales, and course offerings. The US Department of Education and the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) collect and publish comparative data across states but do NOT set a binding national diploma standard.
A_identity.countries_contexts: United States (50 states, DC, territories); American international schools abroad generally follow a similar decentralized, school-specific model rather than one unified 'US curriculum.'
A_identity.qualification_type: State/district-issued secondary school-leaving diploma; no separate national exit exam is required in most states as of current research (some states have their own state-specific assessment/exit-exam requirements, which vary — not verified exhaustively state-by-state in this session).
A_identity.confidence: high — the absence of a single national system is itself extremely well-documented (NCES's own long-running 'State requirements for high school graduation, in Carnegie units' table series exists precisely because there is no single national number to report).

B_grading_model.finding: There is NO single national grading scale. Individual schools/districts set their own scales. Commonly (but NOT universally) seen: numeric 0-100 percentage-based grading on report cards/transcripts, and/or letter grades A-F, converted locally into a GPA — typically on a 4.0 unweighted scale, but weighted scales (commonly 5.0, sometimes 6.0) that add bonus points for Honors (commonly +0.5) and AP/IB/dual-enrollment (commonly +1.0, sometimes +2.0 on 6.0 scales) are widespread and vary district-to-district with no standardizing body. Two schools both claiming a '5.0 weighted scale' may compute it differently.
B_grading_model.the_variability_is_the_finding: This variability is the key, expected, honestly-reported finding for the US system, not a research gap to be resolved — there genuinely is no single answer, confirmed by both NCES's own state-by-state Carnegie-unit tables and by the complete absence of any federal grading-scale regulation.
B_grading_model.college_response_to_variability: Because of this variability, many US colleges do not simply use the transcript-printed GPA; they routinely recompute an applicant's GPA using their own internal methodology (commonly stripping weighting and recalculating on a clean unweighted 4.0 basis) specifically to make cross-school comparisons possible — itself confirming that the raw weighted GPA number is not directly comparable school-to-school without knowing the local scale.
B_grading_model.explicit_rule_reminder: ORYN's existing rule (never force a grade into a 4.0 GPA) is directly validated by this research even for domestic US records — a transcript-printed 'GPA' is not a stable, portable unit unless its scale (gpa_scale field) and weighting status are also known and preserved.

C_structure_concepts.credit_system: The Carnegie unit (a standardized measure of instructional time, roughly one year-long course meeting daily) is the traditional basis for counting credits toward graduation, tracked historically by NCES.

state_variability_examples.texas: Texas mandates a specific statewide default program (the 'Foundation High School Program') requiring a minimum of 22 credits, per the Texas Education Agency (TEA) — a comparatively prescriptive, state-uniform model with defined subject-area minimums (e.g., 4 English credits).
state_variability_examples.california: California's Education Code sets only specific state-minimum COURSE requirements (e.g., 3 years English, 2 years math including Algebra I, 3 years social studies, 2 years science, 1 year of a language/arts/CTE elective) but explicitly leaves the TOTAL number of credit units required for graduation to individual local school districts, per the California Department of Education — most CA public high schools end up requiring the equivalent of 22 to 26 year-long courses, meaning the exact number varies district-by-district WITHIN California itself, not just state-to-state.
state_variability_examples.national_range: Per NCES/Education Commission of the States data, total required units nationally range from roughly 13 units in some states up to 26 units in Texas's older maximal pathway, and three states (Colorado, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania) have historically had NO statewide minimum Carnegie-unit requirement at all, relying instead on state assessments or locally/district-set requirements.

C_structure_concepts.confidence: high on the general pattern (multiple independent primary state-agency sources — TEA, CDE — directly confirm real, structurally different approaches between just these two large states); the 'no statewide minimum' claim for Colorado/MA/PA and the precise national 13-26 unit range are sourced from an NCES-derived secondary summary (Education Commission of the States) rather than freshly re-verified against each state's current primary regulation in this session, so flagged medium confidence on those exact figures/currency.
C_structure_concepts.no_single_national_requirement: Do not assume any single 'typical' US graduation requirement — always treat this as state/district-specific and, where possible, read the actual requirement of the specific school/state in the student's record rather than assuming a national norm.

D_rigor_signals.scope_note: Per this research brief's own instruction, AP/IB/Dual-Enrollment coursework itself is being covered by other agents' work; this section focuses on what is specific to the standard US diploma track's OWN internal rigor culture, separate from those specific credentials.
D_rigor_signals.weighted_gpa_as_rigor_signal: Because weighted GPA scales exist specifically to reward students for taking Honors/AP/IB/dual-enrollment courses relative to their own school's standard track, the GAP between a student's weighted and unweighted GPA (when both are known) is itself a locally-meaningful rigor signal — but only interpretable relative to that specific school's own weighting policy, never across schools without normalization.
D_rigor_signals.class_rank_culture: Historically, US high schools have had a strong class-rank culture (see F below) as an additional native rigor/relative-standing signal, though this is declining and increasingly unpublished at many schools — see F for sourced detail.
D_rigor_signals.school_profile_context: US counselor practice conventionally supplies colleges with a 'school profile' document contextualizing a given school's own grading scale, weighting policy, and course offerings alongside any individual transcript — implying that rigor in the US system is inherently meant to be read RELATIVE TO the specific school's own offerings and norms, not as an absolute cross-school number.
D_rigor_signals.no_oryn_score_invented: No ORYN-internal numeric rigor score is proposed; this section only identifies which native signals (weighted-vs-unweighted GPA gap, class rank where present, and the school-profile-relative reading convention) are meaningful.

E_predicted_grades.finding: Not applicable / not a formal concept in the US system for domestic use. A US transcript shows actual grades-to-date (completed courses through whichever term is current), not a formal prediction of a future final grade — this is a structural difference from IB/A-Level systems, not a data gap.
E_predicted_grades.cross_border_nuance: Predicted grades become relevant only when a US student applies to universities in countries that require them (e.g., is not typically required for domestic US-to-US applications, since senior-year US applicants submit their actual grades-to-date directly and colleges make decisions based on that in-progress transcript plus counselor recommendation, not a separate formal numeric prediction).
E_predicted_grades.confidence: high — this is a clean, well-corroborated 'not applicable' finding, exactly as the research brief anticipated, and should be reported honestly as such rather than forced to resemble the IB/A-Level pattern.

F_class_rank.finding: Class rank IS a historically common feature of the US system, but is genuinely in decline and increasingly optional/unpublished — this is a real, sourced trend, not just an assumption.
F_class_rank.quantified_trend: Per NACAC (National Association for College Admission Counseling) data referenced across multiple sources: the share of colleges rating class rank as having 'considerable importance' in admissions dropped from roughly 42% (2006) to about 9% (2023); over 50% of US high schools now do not report class rankings at all; the average share of applicants submitting class rank to colleges declined roughly 10 percentage points between 2007–2017 overall, with steeper declines (14-22 points) at more selective/Ivy-Plus institutions.
F_class_rank.critical_nuance: A school NOT reporting class rank does not necessarily mean the school doesn't internally calculate/track it — many schools that compute it internally have deliberately stopped PUBLISHING it (to individual students or to colleges) specifically because of its declining admissions weight and concerns about competitive pressure — so 'no rank on this transcript' should be read as 'not published,' not necessarily as 'not computed' or as evidence the school lacks the data at all.
F_class_rank.oryn_rule_reminder: Never infer or fabricate a US student's class rank from GPA alone. Where a transcript is silent on rank, treat it as unknown/not-provided, consistent with the now-common practice of non-publication, rather than assuming its absence signals anything else about the student's standing.

G_external_assessment.finding: There is no single national school-leaving exam comparable to the French Bac exams or German Abiturprüfung. The closest external, standardized assessments most US students encounter are the SAT and ACT — but these are college-admissions tests administered by independent nonprofit organizations (College Board for SAT; ACT, Inc. for the ACT), NOT part of the high school diploma or transcript system itself, and a student can earn a full US diploma without ever sitting either. Per this brief's own instruction, SAT/ACT data should be tracked as separate evidence (ORYN's existing generic test_scores table) rather than folded into curriculum/diploma documentation — the relationship to note is simply that they are optional, separately-administered, admissions-oriented assessments layered on top of (not part of) the diploma system.
G_external_assessment.state_exit_exams_caveat: Some individual states have historically imposed their OWN state-specific exit/end-of-course exam requirements for diploma eligibility (separate from SAT/ACT) — this varies by state and was not exhaustively verified state-by-state in this session; flagged as an open/unresolved item rather than asserted as either universal or absent.

H_unsafe_inferences: Do not assume any single 'typical' or 'standard' US GPA scale, graduation-credit count, or grading convention — always defer to the specific school/state/district's own stated scale (gpa_scale field) rather than assuming 4.0/100-point defaults.

Do not assume a missing/unpublished class rank means the school doesn't track it internally — non-publication has become the common practice at over half of US high schools specifically because of declining admissions weight, not because tracking stopped.
Do not conflate SAT/ACT scores with the high school diploma/curriculum system — they are separate, optional, externally-administered admissions tests, not a diploma component.

Do not assume weighted GPA figures are comparable across different schools/districts without knowing each school's specific weighting policy (bonus-point amounts and which course categories qualify vary with no standardizing body).

Do not assume predicted grades are a meaningful/expected data point for a US-educated student's domestic record — the concept is largely inapplicable outside of that student's own applications to non-US institutions.

Do not assume every state's graduation-requirement structure resembles Texas's prescriptive statewide model — some states (e.g., California) delegate significant portions of the requirement (total unit count) down to local districts, and a few historically had no statewide minimum at all.

should_care_about: The specific school's own grading scale and GPA weighting policy (via gpa_scale and notes) before drawing any conclusion from overall_gpa.
The gap between weighted and unweighted GPA where both are known, read relative to that school's own weighting rules — not as an absolute cross-school figure.
Class rank ONLY when explicitly present in the record, read with awareness that its absence is now the norm at most US schools and does not itself imply anything about the student.
The specific state/district's stated graduation requirements as context for how much of a 'standard load' a given transcript represents, since there is no universal baseline.
should_not_do: Force a single implied national GPA/credit standard onto every US record.
Fabricate or infer a class rank when the transcript is silent.
Treat SAT/ACT scores as part of the diploma/curriculum evidence rather than as separate test_scores evidence.
Assume a predicted-grade data point should exist for a domestic US applicant.

J_profile_data_model_implications.fits_existing_schema_how: education_records.curriculum has no explicit 'us_high_school_diploma' value; unlike the French/German case, mapping a plain US diploma to 'national_curriculum' is arguably MORE misleading here than for France/Germany, because the US genuinely has no national curriculum at all — 'other' may actually be the more honest current fit, or a dedicated enum value would remove the ambiguity entirely. overall_gpa and gpa_scale (both present and correctly generic/numeric) are actually well-suited to the US case AS LONG AS gpa_scale is always populated accurately per-school (e.g., 4.0, 4.3, 4.5, 5.0, 6.0, or 100) rather than defaulted — this is the schema's biggest working strength for the US case, since it already supports scale preservation without forced conversion, consistent with ORYN's existing no-cross-conversion rule.
gaps: No field to record whether a given overall_gpa value is WEIGHTED or UNWEIGHTED — this is a materially important, US-specific gap: two students both showing 'gpa_scale=5.0, overall_gpa=4.6' could represent very different rigor levels, or the same rigor level reported differently, depending on weighting policy, and the schema currently cannot distinguish this without relying on free-text notes.

No explicit curriculum enum value for a plain US diploma track — currently must default to 'national_curriculum' (semantically inaccurate, since no such national curriculum exists) or 'other' (semantically honest but uninformative/indistinguishable from any other unclassified system).

No structured field for class rank AT ALL in education_records — given how central (if declining) a signal this historically is/was in the US system specifically, and given the explicit product rule to never infer it, a dedicated nullable class_rank / class_size / rank_reported_boolean field (rather than only relying on notes) could reduce the risk of a future implementation accidentally inferring or omitting this distinction inconsistently. This is offered as a genuine, worth-flagging design consideration for Claude B, not a demand — 'national_curriculum + notes' can technically capture it today, just with more inference risk than a dedicated field would carry.

The precise current (2026) status of the 'no statewide minimum Carnegie-unit requirement' claim for Colorado, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania was sourced from an NCES-derived secondary summary (Education Commission of the States) rather than freshly re-checked against each state's current primary regulation — recommend a follow-up direct check against each state's Department of Education if this specific claim becomes product-critical.

No comprehensive state-by-state enumeration of exact weighted-GPA bonus-point conventions (which vary widely) was attempted in this session beyond the commonly-cited +0.5/Honors, +1.0/AP-IB pattern — this pattern should be treated as illustrative/common, not exhaustive or universal.
